slides.text:
A map stores values that you find by a key instead of by a position. It is how Go keeps things like a price for each product or a score for each player.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.

In this module you will create maps, add and change entries, look up a key that is not there, and remove entries. Then you will see nil maps and what happens when a map is shared with a function. Key and value types come in the next module, and ways of using maps to solve problems after it.

Every entry of a map is a pair: a key and the value stored under it. All keys have one type and all values have one type, and the map type names both.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
map from text to number
    key: text
    value: number

slides.text: A map has no order and no positions. A key appears at most once, and writing to a key that exists replaces its value. Printing a map with `fmt` lists the entries sorted by key, so the output is always the same.

`make` is the built-in you already used for slices. For a map, it gives an empty map that is ready to write to. A map that is only declared is **nil**, and writing to it fails: session 2 explains it.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
stock = make(map from text to number)
stock is empty and ready
stock[key] = value  -> adds an entry

slides.text:
A map that is declared but never made is **nil**. It has no storage yet. Reading it, asking its `len` and deleting from it all work and behave like an empty map, but writing to it stops the program with a panic.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
maps
    declared only -> nil
        read   -> zero value
        write  -> panic
    made          -> ready
        write  -> works

slides.text: `make` and a literal like `map[string]int{}` both give a map that is ready to write to. A nil map is a trap when a map is declared in one place and filled in another, so make it before the first write.

exercises.title: Declare without make
exercises.guide: See what a map that was never made can do.

chunks.guide: A `var` with a map type and no value gives a nil map. It prints like an empty one.

notes.text: Only a nil map is equal to nil.

chunks.text:
var ages map[string]int
    fmt.Println(ages == nil, len(ages), ages)

chunks.guide: Reading a key of a nil map is fine and gives the zero value.
Deleting from a nil map does nothing and is not an error.

exercises.title: Make before writing
exercises.guide: Turn a nil map into one you can write to.

chunks.guide: Declared and never made, so it is nil.
After `make` the variable holds a real map, and the write works. The variable already exists, so use `=`.
It is not nil anymore.

exercises.title: Ready to write
exercises.guide: Make the map only when it is still nil, then print how many entries it has.

exercises.title: Does it have an error?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what happens.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var stock map[string]int
    fmt.Println(stock["a"])
    stock["a"] = 1
    fmt.Println(stock)
}
options: No error, it prints 0 and map[a:1]
A compile error on the read
A panic at the write, after printing 0
A compile error on the write
exercises.explanation: The program compiles. The read of a nil map gives 0, and the write panics when it runs, so the second print never happens.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var unset map[string]int
    literal := map[string]int{}
    made := make(map[string]int)
    literal["x"] = 1
    made["y"]++
    fmt.Println(unset == nil, literal == nil,
        len(unset), len(literal), len(made))
}
exercises.explanation: Only `unset` was never made, so only `unset` is nil. All three have a `len` and the two made maps took one entry each.

slides.text:
An array is copied when you assign it or pass it to a function. A map is not: the variable holds a reference to the entries, so a copy of the variable looks at the **same** entries.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
a is a map -> entries x:1
b = a   -> b sees the same entries
b sets x = 9 -> a sees x = 9

slides.text:
The same goes for a function. It can add, change and delete entries of the caller's map. What it cannot do is replace the caller's variable: giving its own parameter a new map only changes its own copy.

To get an independent map, make a new one and copy the entries into it.

notes.text: The whole map type, with no length.
